q: Statement I: Heavy rain fell in the northern hills for three days. Statement II: The river flooded villages downstream. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
x: Days of heavy rain upstream raise the river's water, which then floods villages downstream. The rain comes first and produces the flood.

q: Statement I: The price of petrol rose sharply across the country. Statement II: Bus fares in the city were increased. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are independent causes
x: Buses run on fuel, so a sharp rise in fuel prices raises their running costs and leads to higher fares. The fare rise follows from the petrol price rise.

q: Statement I: Most students in the class failed the physics test. Statement II: The physics teacher was absent for most of the term and no replacement was arranged. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: With no one teaching physics for most of the term, students were poorly prepared and failed. The teacher's absence (statement II) led to the result (statement I).

q: Statement I: All shops in the city remained closed on Friday. Statement II: Public transport did not run in the city on Friday. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: Closed shops do not stop buses, and stopped buses do not explain every shop closing. Both point to one shared cause, such as a strike or public holiday that day.

q: Statement I: Many students in the hostel fell ill soon after dinner. Statement II: The hostel cook also fell ill after tasting the same meal. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: The students' illness did not make the cook ill, nor the other way round. Both became ill from one shared cause: the contaminated meal they all ate.

q: Statement I: The college cricket team won the inter-college trophy. Statement II: The college canteen raised the price of tea. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: A cricket win has nothing to do with the price of tea, and neither event explains the other. Each has its own separate cause.

q: Statement I: Rice exports from the country rose this year. Statement II: A new metro line opened in the capital this year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are independent causes
x: Rice exports depend on harvests and world demand; a metro line depends on city planning. The events are unrelated results of separate causes.

q: Statement I: Several cars skidded off the hill road on Sunday afternoon. Statement II: An hour earlier, a tanker had spilled oil across the same hill road. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: Oil on a road makes it slippery, so cars lose grip and skid. The spill (statement II) happened first and led to the skidding (statement I).

q: Statement I: The government doubled the tax on cigarettes. Statement II: Sales of cigarettes fell over the next six months. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: Doubling the tax raises the price of cigarettes, and higher prices reduce how many people buy. The tax rise came first and caused the drop in sales.

q: Statement I: Many patients came to city clinics with fever and joint pain in October. Statement II: The city had standing rainwater for weeks after the monsoon, and mosquito numbers rose sharply. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are independent causes
x: Standing water lets mosquitoes breed, and mosquitoes spread illnesses such as dengue that cause fever and joint pain. The conditions in statement II led to the cases in statement I.

q: A lift stopped between two floors, and at the same moment every light in the building went off. Which single cause explains both facts?
o: Too many people inside the lift
A power failure in the building
A passenger pressing the wrong button
The lift doors getting jammed
x: Only a power failure explains both the lift stopping and every light in the building going off. Overloading or a jammed door would affect the lift alone.

q: Hamza's bicycle tyre was full of air in the evening but flat next morning, and he found a nail stuck in it. What is the most likely cause?
o: The nail punctured the tyre and the air leaked out
The cold night air froze the tyre
The tyre had been pumped too hard
Someone borrowed the bicycle overnight
x: A nail through the tyre makes a hole, and the air slowly escapes. The other reasons do not account for the nail found in the tyre.

q: Bread from the same bakery, stored in the same way, goes mouldy within two days in July but lasts about a week in January. What is the most likely cause?
o: The bread is cheaper in July
Warm, humid weather in July helps mould grow faster
Customers buy more bread in January
The shop opens later in July
x: Mould grows faster in warmth and moisture, which July has and January lacks. Price, sales and opening hours have no effect on how fast bread spoils.

q: In a hostel, 20 students got food poisoning on Sunday. All 20 had eaten chicken curry at lunch. Students who skipped the curry but ate the same rice and salad stayed well. What is the most likely cause?
o: The rice was contaminated
The salad was contaminated
The Sunday weather was very hot
The chicken curry was contaminated
x: Only the curry is common to every ill student and missing for those who stayed well. The rice and salad were eaten by healthy students too, so they are unlikely causes.

q: A phone worked perfectly until it was dropped into a bucket of water; after that, its screen and buttons stopped responding. What is the most likely cause?
o: The mobile network went down
Water got inside the phone and damaged its circuits
The phone's memory became full
The SIM card expired
x: The fault began straight after the phone was in water, and water inside a phone can short its circuits. A network, memory or SIM problem would not stop the screen and buttons responding.

q: After the streetlights on one stretch of a highway were removed, accidents on that stretch rose sharply, but only at night. Accidents on other stretches did not change. What is the most likely cause?
o: Heavier rainfall over the whole highway
Younger drivers using the whole highway
More traffic police on the other stretches
Poor visibility at night on the unlit stretch
x: The rise is limited to the unlit stretch and to night-time, exactly where and when the missing lights matter. Rain or driver age would affect the whole highway, not just that stretch at night.

q: A student believes that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Mirrors are expensive to replace
There is no evidence or known way that a broken mirror can affect future events
Many people share this belief
Glass breaks very easily
x: A broken mirror is only broken glass; nothing connects it to later events, and no evidence shows such a link. The other statements do not address whether the belief is true.

q: Rashid says, "Every time I wash my car, it rains the next day, so washing my car causes rain." Which is a valid reason to reject his claim?
o: Rashid should wash his car less often
Rain depends on weather systems, and he probably remembers only the times the two happened together
Cars get dirty again in the rain
It rains more during the monsoon
x: Washing a car cannot change the weather, and people tend to remember the coincidences and forget the dry days. The other options do not show that the claim is false.

q: Some people think the number 13 is unlucky. Which is a valid argument that a hospital's 13th floor is no more dangerous than any other floor?
o: A floor's number is only a label; it does not change the building or the care given there
Thirteen is an odd number
Most hospitals skip the 13th floor
The 13th floor is higher than the 12th
x: Safety depends on the building and the staff, not on the number painted on a floor. Naming or skipping floors does not change any real condition.

q: A man says a lucky stone cured his fever, because he wore it for three days and the fever went away. Which is the best reason to reject his claim?
o: The stone was very expensive
Stones are found everywhere
He bought the stone from a famous shop
Many fevers go away on their own within a few days, so the stone may have had no effect
x: Recovery after wearing the stone does not show the stone caused it, because many fevers end on their own. Price or place of purchase says nothing about whether the stone works.

q: A neighbour says that a solar eclipse makes cooked food poisonous, so all food should be thrown away afterwards. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Eclipses happen only rarely
During an eclipse the Moon only blocks sunlight for a short time; it adds nothing harmful to food
Scientists like to study eclipses
Throwing food away is a waste of money
x: An eclipse simply means the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth, briefly cutting off sunlight. Nothing in this process can make food poisonous. Wasting money is a cost, not proof that the belief is false.

q: A cricket fan believes his team loses whenever he watches its matches live on TV. Which is a valid reason to reject his belief?
o: His TV set is very old
The team has lost many matches
He could listen on the radio instead
His watching cannot affect the players, whose results depend on skill and conditions on the field
x: A viewer at home has no way to influence the play. The team's results depend on the players and the match conditions, so his watching is not a cause.

q: A report finds that in towns where more umbrellas are sold, more people catch colds. Someone concludes that umbrellas cause colds. Which fact best shows the conclusion is false?
o: Umbrellas cost more in big towns
Umbrella shops open early in the morning
Cold, rainy weather increases both umbrella sales and the number of colds
Most umbrellas are made in factories
x: A third factor, cold rainy weather, drives both figures up. When one cause produces two effects, the effects move together without one causing the other.

q: Some people believe that an owl hooting near a house means someone inside will fall ill. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Owls hoot to call to each other and while hunting; their calls cannot cause illness
Owls are seldom seen in daytime
Many people are afraid of owls
Owls live in old trees
x: An owl's call is ordinary bird behaviour, and illness is caused by things such as germs, not by sounds of birds. Fear of owls does not make the belief true.

q: "My uncle smoked all his life and lived to 90, so smoking is not harmful." Why is this argument not valid?
o: The uncle was a wealthy man
Ninety is not a great age
One person's case cannot outweigh evidence from studies of very large numbers of smokers
Cigarettes are expensive
x: Large studies show smoking raises the risk of serious diseases; a single lucky person does not cancel that evidence. A risk means more people are harmed, not that every person is.

q: A student thinks exams on Tuesdays bring him bad results, because his last two Tuesday exams went badly. Which is a valid reason to reject this belief?
o: Two cases are far too few, and his results more likely depended on his preparation and the papers
Tuesday is a short working day
He should study harder on Mondays
Exams are always difficult
x: Two poor results are not enough to show a pattern, and the day of the week has no way to affect marks. Preparation and paper difficulty are the real factors.

q: A farmer says his crop was excellent this year because he sowed it on a 'lucky' date. That year rainfall was good, and he also used better seed. Which is the best argument against his claim?
o: Lucky dates are different for each person
Crops grow every year anyway
The good rainfall and better seed explain the harvest, and a date by itself cannot affect plant growth
He should have sown earlier
x: Two real causes of a good crop, water and seed quality, were present. Plants respond to conditions such as water and soil, not to the calendar, so the date adds nothing to the explanation.

q: Zainab started using a new pen and got a headache the same day, so she blames the pen. Which is a valid reason to doubt her conclusion?
o: The pen was very cheap
She could have used a pencil
Headaches are painful
Two things happening on the same day does not prove that one caused the other
x: The headache may have come from lack of sleep, stress or many other things. Happening at the same time is not enough to show the pen was the cause.

q: Some people believe an itchy palm means money is coming. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Many people believe this
Itching is caused by things such as dry skin or insect bites, which have no link with income
Money is hard to earn
Palms often get dirty
x: Itching has physical causes in the skin. Nothing connects these causes to future income, and popular belief does not make a claim true.

q: Bilal says, "Since I started drinking milk at night, my marks have improved, so milk improved my marks." Which fact, if true, most weakens his claim?
o: Milk contains calcium
He began attending extra classes at the same time
His friend drinks tea at night
His marks are given as percentages
x: If extra classes started at the same time, they offer another cause for the better marks. The milk can no longer be singled out as the reason.

q: Which of the following is a valid cause-and-effect claim rather than a superstition?
o: Leaving milk out of the fridge in summer makes it go sour faster
Sweeping the floor at night drives wealth away
A crow cawing on the roof means a guest will arrive
Shaking your legs brings bad luck
x: Warmth lets bacteria in milk multiply faster, so it sours sooner; this is a real cause. The others claim links that have no possible mechanism or evidence.

q: Some people say walking under a ladder brings bad luck. Which reason for not walking under a ladder is logically valid?
o: It brings misfortune for the rest of the day
Ladders are made of wood or metal
A tool or paint could fall on you from the ladder
Most people avoid walking under ladders
x: Falling objects are a real, physical danger near a ladder in use. Bad luck has no cause behind it, and what most people do is not a reason.

q: Ayesha failed her first driving test and says, "I will never be able to drive." Which is the strongest argument to change her belief?
o: Driving is not an important skill
One failure shows what she needs to practise; driving skill improves with practice, and the test can be taken again
Several of her friends also failed
She should give up and use buses instead
x: One result does not prove a permanent limit; it points to the skills she must practise. Others failing or driving being unimportant does not answer her belief.

q: Statement I: The village set up a plant to filter its drinking water. Statement II: Cases of diarrhoea in the village fell over the next year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: Diarrhoea is often spread by germs in dirty water. Clean filtered water removes that cause, so the fall in cases follows from the new plant.

q: Statement I: Pass rates in the district's girls' schools rose sharply. Statement II: The district appointed trained teachers to every girls' school that had empty teaching posts. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are independent causes
x: Filling empty posts with trained teachers means students are properly taught, which raises pass rates. Statement II came first and led to statement I.

q: Statement I: Volunteers planted thousands of trees along the canal banks. Statement II: The canal banks were worn away much less in the following monsoon. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
x: Tree roots hold the soil together, so the banks resist being washed away by flowing water. The planting came first and caused the reduced erosion.

q: Statement I: A student from Quetta won a national science prize. Statement II: A new hospital opened in Multan. Which of the following is correct?
o: Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: The two events are in different cities and neither leads to the other. Each happened for its own separate reasons.

q: Bilal says his poor results are his fate and nothing he does can change them. Which argument most strongly shows his belief is false?
o: Fate is talked about in many stories
Some of his classmates also get poor results
His marks improved in the past whenever he studied regularly, so his effort clearly affects his results
He should stop worrying about results
x: His own record shows that changing his study habits changed his marks. That evidence directly contradicts the claim that nothing he does matters.

q: Statement: Should students form study groups before exams? Argument I: Yes, explaining topics to each other helps students understand them better. Argument II: No, because one group once wasted its time chatting.
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a general, relevant benefit of study groups. Argument II rests on a single case, which is not enough to judge study groups as a whole.

q: After several accidents on a sharp bend, villagers say the bend is 'cursed'. Which response is both logical and helpful?
o: Everyone should avoid the road for ever
The accidents happen because the drivers are unlucky
Nothing can be done about a cursed bend
The accidents are better explained by the sharp turn and high speed; warning signs and speed breakers would reduce them
x: Sharp bends with poor visibility and speeding are real causes of accidents. Naming the real cause leads to a fix, while 'curse' and 'bad luck' explain nothing.

q: Statement I: The college hockey team performed far better this season. Statement II: At the start of the season, the team began daily training with a qualified coach. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: Regular coached training improves skill and fitness, which shows in better results. The training (statement II) came first and caused the improvement (statement I).

q: Statement: Should young people be encouraged to volunteer in hospitals? Argument I: Yes, it gives them experience of caring for others and helps hospitals with simple tasks. Argument II: Yes, because volunteering guarantees them admission to medical college.
o: Only argument I is strong
Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives real benefits to both the young people and the hospitals. Argument II makes a false promise, since volunteering guarantees no one a college seat.

q: Some people in a poor area say, "We will always be poor, so building a school here is pointless." Which is the strongest counter-argument?
o: Schools are only buildings
Education builds skills that help people find better work, so a school can reduce poverty over time
Other areas are poor too
Poverty is decided by fate
x: The claim assumes poverty cannot change, but education gives people skills for better-paid work. That is a direct, strong reason to build the school.

q: Statement I: A factory fitted filters to its chimneys to trap smoke. Statement II: Complaints of coughing and breathing trouble from people living nearby fell over the next year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are independent causes
x: Filters cut the smoke released into the air, and cleaner air means fewer breathing problems for neighbours. The filters came first and caused the fall in complaints.

q: Statement I: The broken streetlights in the market were repaired. Statement II: Thefts in the market at night fell sharply after that. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
x: Well-lit streets make it harder for thieves to act unseen. The repair came first and led to fewer night-time thefts.

q: Statement I: Far fewer children in the town missed school because of illness this year. Statement II: At the start of this year, every school in the town began providing clean drinking water and soap for hand-washing. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
x: Clean water and hand-washing cut the spread of germs that cause common childhood illnesses, so fewer days are missed. The measures in statement II came first and caused the effect in statement I.

q: Statement: Should citizens who help road accident victims be given public awards? Argument I: Yes, awards would encourage more people to help in emergencies. Argument II: No, because helpers might get their clothes dirty.
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a relevant reason linked to saving lives. Argument II is trivial and has nothing to do with whether awards are a good idea.
